newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK MANUFACTURING SUFFERS FROM DUTCH DISEASE-SPRAOS.
newsitem.headline: GREEK MANUFACTURING SUFFERS FROM DUTCH DISEASE-SPRAOS.

text.p: The drachma's real appreciation is the main cause behind the declining share of manufacturing in Greece's GDP over the last 20 years -- the Dutch disease --, said economics professor Yannis Spraos in a working paper.
Spraos is an advisor to Prime Minister Costas Simitis.

"The underdevelopment of manufacturing is not due to Greeks' low consumption of manufactured goods as shown by the large net imports of manufactured products," said Spraos. "The obvious explanation is the Dutch disease."

The Dutch disease refers to a phenomenon where a favourable change in conditions affecting one tradable sector can adversely affect other tradable sectors by squeezing their profits or the returns to specific production factors.
The name 'Dutch disease' was given after the rapid development of the natural gas producing sector in Holland resulted in a squeeze on other traditional export sectors.
Another example of the Dutch disease was the strengthening of the pound on anticipation of future oil revenues from North Sea discoveries that hurt British manufacturers of export goods.
Forex inflows from tourism, remmitances, shipping as well as the European Union led to the real appreciation of the drachma and hurt the competitiveness of Greek manufacturing, said Spraos.
His working paper is titled "How we caught the Dutch disease and must we or may we be cured? Thoughts on the role of manufacturing."
"You might tell me: It is the incomes policy and the hard drachma policy that have to be blamed," said Spraos in his working paper. "I would answer, you are marginally right-- but only marginally."

The exchange rate policy has a short-term impact but cannot go against the tide of forex flows in the long-term, said Spaos who is the leading candidate to become Greece's ambassador to the IMF, sources say.
He said investment laws and the small-size of Greek firms also accounted for the loss of competitiveness in manufacturing.
Greece's investment laws should be revised to offer more differentiated incentives based on comparative advantages that will favour high return investments.

Greek firms should also try to grow in size and mergers offered a convenient vehicle, said the professor who helped spook the bourse with a recent proposal for a one-off 10 percent surcharge on corporate profits in 1998. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
